Thank you for the opportunity to share my thoughts. I found the questions about sensitive data types quite challenging, especially when considering the trade-offs between privacy and identification accuracy.

For me, the most important question was Q5.2, where we had unanimous agreement on prioritizing equal recall across groups. Ensuring that all students have an equal chance of being identified and receiving support is crucial for fairness in student success.

I noticed a significant difference in opinions regarding the use of Absalon data (Q3.4), with many opting for "never" acceptable. I understand privacy concerns, but I believe that with proper consent and clear communication about data usage, this could be a valuable source of information for identifying students who need support earlier. Perhaps an opt-in mechanism could address these concerns?

Thank you for sharing your perspective.

I also found the questions around sensitive data types quite challenging, particularly Q3.5 and Q3.6. Determining the minimum improvement needed to justify the use of such data was difficult because it involves balancing privacy concerns with the potential benefits of early intervention.

For me, the most critical question is Q4.1, specifically the trade-offs between explainability and accuracy. High explainability is essential for building trust with students and advisors alike. It ensures that we can understand why a student is flagged and provide appropriate support tailored to their needs.

I was surprised by the unanimous agreement on never using race/ethnicity data (Q3.5.race_ethnicity), even if it improves identification or fairness. While I share these concerns, I wonder if there are specific contexts where this data might be crucial for addressing systemic inequities. For instance, certain ethnic groups might face unique challenges that a model could help identify. An opt-out mechanism could mitigate some of the privacy issues associated with using such data.

I think Q5.2 is crucial—equal recall across groups ensures fairness. It surprised me that everyone agreed on this; perhaps because we all want equitable support systems.

For sensitive data (Q3.5, Q3.6), I leaned toward "never" for most types due to privacy concerns. However, if financial aid status could help identify at-risk students, an opt-in mechanism might make it acceptable.

Lastly, on explainability (Q4.1), I agree that moderate improvements are worth the trade-off for better support, but transparency is key to trust. Maybe we can explore ways to communicate these decisions clearly with students?
